contract: A short front desk notice. From March 3, holds on new-release DVDs expire after 4 days instead of 7. Holds on books, audiobooks and magazines stay at 7 days. The source records no reason for the change, so the notice gives none. The Elm Street shelf overflow is a separate remark; the notice may repeat it as a separate item or leave it out, and never presents it as the cause or circumstance of the change. The vote (5 to 2, February meeting) may be kept or omitted, and if kept it stays accurate.
supported_facts: Starting March 3, holds on new-release DVDs expire after 4 days instead of 7.
The circulation committee voted for the change at the February meeting, 5 to 2.
The minutes do not say why; nobody explained the reasoning.
Holds on books, audiobooks and magazines are not affected and stay at 7 days.
Separately, the Elm Street hold shelf has been overflowing since January.
invented_facts_that_fail: Any reason or purpose for the shorter DVD hold, such as more turnover or shorter waits.
The Elm Street shelf overflow presented as the cause or circumstance of the change.
A claim that the committee or the minutes gave a reason.
The 4 day rule applied to all holds, or to books, audiobooks or magazines.
A different start date, vote count or meeting month.
legitimate_alternatives: Say plainly that no reason was recorded, or say nothing about a reason.
Drop the vote count and meeting, or keep them accurately.
Mention the Elm Street shelf as a separate item, or omit it.
Use a list, a heading or one paragraph.

judgments.question: Does the notice say new-release DVD holds expire after 4 days?
Does the notice keep the March 3 start date?
Does the notice keep book, audiobook and magazine holds at 7 days, with no claim that all holds changed?
If the vote or meeting is mentioned, is it the February meeting and 5 to 2?
Does the notice avoid claiming a reason was recorded or explained?
Does the notice avoid giving any reason for the change, including linking it to the Elm Street shelf?

examples.label: valid
examples.text: Front desk notice: Starting March 3, holds on new-release DVDs expire after 4 days instead of 7. The circulation committee approved the change 5 to 2 at its February meeting; the minutes don't record a reason. Holds on books, audiobooks and magazines are unchanged at 7 days.

examples.label: valid
examples.text:
Notice for front desk staff

From March 3, new-release DVD holds expire after four days (it was seven). Book, audiobook and magazine holds still expire after 7 days.

Separately, the Elm Street hold shelf has been overflowing since January.

examples.label: failing
examples.text: Starting March 3, holds on new-release DVDs expire after 4 days instead of 7, so that more patrons get a turn with popular titles. Holds on books, audiobooks and magazines stay at 7 days.

examples.label: failing
examples.text: Starting March 3, new-release DVD holds expire after 4 days instead of 7. The Elm Street hold shelf has been overflowing since January, which is why the committee voted 5 to 2 for the change. Book, audiobook and magazine holds stay at 7 days.
examples.note: Two adjacent statements joined into a cause the source never states.

examples.label: failing
examples.text: Starting March 3, all holds expire after 4 days instead of 7. The committee approved it 5 to 2 in February.
examples.note: Broadens the DVD rule to every hold.

examples.label: failing
examples.text: Starting March 10, holds on new-release DVDs expire after 4 days instead of 7. Book holds stay at 7 days.

examples.label: failing
examples.text: Starting March 3, new-release DVD holds expire after 4 days instead of 7. The committee explained its reasoning at the February meeting. Book, audiobook and magazine holds stay at 7 days.
examples.note: Uses only source words to state the opposite of the source.
